$comment: Being out of someone's reach: they hold no power to change your duties. Diplomatic immunity is one. Judicial immunity — a judge cannot be sued for what they did on the bench — is one. Constitutional rights are the large case: even a legislature holding enormous power cannot touch certain positions, and only changing the charter itself would let it. Prefixed because 'immunity' alone is the biological sense, and the enterprise means both — though the legal sense came first: immunis is in- plus munus, exempt from duty. An immunity is not a liberty. A liberty says you do no wrong by acting; an immunity says someone else cannot reach you.

name.$comment: What the immunity is called, as it is said.

under.$comment: The authority that establishes it. An immunity holds because something structural says so, so the thing that says so is what would have to change for it to lapse.

protects.$comment: The duty that cannot be changed. Names an obligation and not a work: an immunity is about the reach of others over your position, not about anything you do.

against.$comment: Who cannot reach you. They are correspondingly disabled — they simply lack the power. An immunity against nobody names no one who is thereby stopped, and so stops nothing.

$comment-absences: No discharged-when: an immunity is held, not discharged. It is a standing fact about what others cannot do, not an obligation with a settling condition. No holder or bearer: the office's deontic profile is where the holder enters.
